newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mystery American wins world's biggest pigeon race.
newsitem.headline: Mystery American wins world's biggest pigeon race.

text.p: A mystery American living in London was $250,000 dollars richer on Saturday when a pigeon he sponsored was first back to the loft in the world's richest homing race.

David Barlow's aptly named bird "It's Worth A Flutter" was first through the traps at South Africa's luxury Sun City resort 160 km (100 miles) northwest of Johannesburg after averaging 87 kph (53 mph) for nearly seven hours in the World Free Flight race.

Organisers gave Barlow's name and a London telephone number, but there was no further details about the winning entrant -- whether he was among avid international pigeon fanciers who entered an original 1,800-off birds, or merely a "punter" who staked the $1,000 entry fee in a blind gamble.

Pigeons from Belgium, Germany and Taiwan followed Barlow's blue pigeon over the electronic finish line within fractions of a second in the million dollar, 609 (405 mile) event, surprising experts who were caught unawares by the early arrival.
The first two flocks swooped over the lofts and touched down to take the top prizes nearly two hours ahead of the predicted time.
"I must have trained them too well," said chief handler Zandy Meyer of South Africa, who forecast a race of nine hours, rather than the six hours and 54 minutes it took.

Over the past several months, Meyer put the birds, all less than a year old, through 7,000 km of training flights to acclimatise them to their new "home" in specially built lofts at Sun City, to which they would return with an unerring instinct not fully understood by scientists.

By the time of their final release shortly after dawn on Saturday at a lake in central South Africa, only 887 birds were still in the race, braving the risk of African birds of prey and temperatures in the low 30s (90F) to fly home.
"These are some of the finest birds in the world," said fancier Paul Smith of Regency Lofts in England. "And this is by far the biggest prize money ever offered in the sport."
The first 200 birds in the race were due to be auctioned off and fanciers confidently predicted that they would fetch prices of several thousand dollars.
